Pele Yoetz 351:4: And not only is it forbidden to swear by the Name of the Name, but even to swear by one's own soul and life unnecessarily is forbidden, and how much more so to swear falsely, since he thereby injures his own soul. And there are places where people have accustomed their tongues to swear over every single utterance by the life of their father or brother, or by the life of the fellow they are speaking with, and these are matters of disgrace, loss of dignity, and shame, besides the prohibition of vain oaths, for the commentators explained the verse (Deuteronomy 5:11), “You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold guiltless” — even one who takes his own name in vain, and how much more so, and how much more certainly, the Name of the Omnipresent.
Pele Yoetz 351:5: And truly it is foolishness for no purpose — if people will believe, they will believe, and if not, they will not believe; what does it matter to them? And this is the punishment of one habituated to swearing: that people do not believe any of his oaths, unlike one who is not habituated to swearing, so that whenever he is compelled and it is fitting for him to swear — such as when he is suspected of something he did not do and wishes to clear himself, when it is fitting for him to swear so that his words be believed, to fulfill “and you shall be clear”, and in order to satisfy their minds so that they not suspect the innocent — then they shall believe his words and tremble when they hear an oath from his mouth. This is his reward in this world, and in the World to Come, much more so. And “a soul who swears to do something” shall not break his word, whether he swore by the Name, or swore by his own life or soul, or by his father's life or his fellow's life, for if he does not fulfill it, it turns out he treats Heaven's honor lightly, and this shows he has no regard for his Maker's honor, or no regard for his own life, or for his father's life, or his fellow's life — for all this shall God bring into judgment.
Pele Yoetz 351:6: And it is known that a handshake [tekiat kaf, a gesture sealing a commitment] is considered a severe oath and must be fulfilled. And there are several ignorant people among the populace who rule leniently for themselves: when they make oaths and do not wish to fulfill them, they say that it is disadvantageous for them and there is no oath regarding something disadvantageous — and they err regarding what we have established, that an oath does not take effect when one swears to transgress a commandment (Nedarim 16a), but absent that, the obligation requires fulfillment, and the punishment for one who transgresses an oath is severe. Therefore, whatever comes out of his mouth, he must do.
Pele Yoetz 352:1: Shem Shamayim (Heaven's Name) — If one mentions Heaven's Name in vain, he also transgresses (Deuteronomy 5:11), “You shall not take the Name of the Lord your God in vain.” And I have already said that this applies whether he mentions it in the holy tongue or in the languages of the gentiles. And just as one must be careful not to mention the Name Havayah in filthy alleyways or in an unclean place, so one must be careful not to mention it in any language of the gentiles. Therefore one must be careful, when speaking in the bathhouse, not to mention and say “Dio” [God], which is the Name of the Name in the Spanish language. And likewise one should not say the Name (but rather “Rasul Allah” [a substitute phrase]), which is a mention of the Name of the Name in the Ishmaelite [Arabic] language, and so in every language.
Pele Yoetz 352:2: And the halachic authorities already warned that a person should not say to his fellow, “Did you say Eloheinu [our God]?” [referring to a prayer insertion], but rather should say to him, “Did you say Ya'aleh V'Yavo?” And likewise one should not say, “Did you say Elohai Neshamah?” [a prayer beginning “My God, the soul”], which is a mention of the Name in vain, but rather should say, “Did you say the morning blessings?” or say “Elokai” or “Elokeinu” with a kuf [substituting a letter to avoid pronouncing the Name-like word directly]. And likewise those who assist in reciting the blessings for grooms should not begin their assistance from the word “Eloheinu,” but rather from “Melech HaOlam,” and the like. Go and learn how far they were concerned about mentioning the Name in vain, to the point that they said (Nedarim 10b) that a person should not say “to the Lord, an offering,” but rather “an offering to the Lord.” And likewise a person should not say to his fellow, “May the Lord give you good days,” but rather, “Good days may the Lord give you” — this is because of concern that as soon as he mentions the Name, his soul might depart and he could not finish speaking, and it would turn out that he mentioned Heaven's Name in vain. And how many ignorant people, especially among women, commonly mention Heaven's Name in vain over some astonishing thing they see. And how good is the custom of those who fear the Name and esteem His Name, who do not mention Heaven's Name at all, but rather say, “The blessed Name.”
Pele Yoetz 352:3: And one must fear the honored and awesome Name so as not to mention it except in Torah reading, prayers, and blessings, and even in blessings one must be careful about blessings recited in vain, or unnecessary blessings, which are considered a mention of Heaven's Name in vain and transgress “You shall not take.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Nedarim 7b) that one who hears his fellow mention Heaven's Name in vain is obligated to excommunicate him, and if not, he himself shall be under a ban. And they explained that this means: the one who hears and does not excommunicate shall be under a ban. Therefore one should be careful to say to himself, “May you be released from the ban, released from the ban, released from the ban.” Go and learn the severity involved.
Pele Yoetz 352:4: And included in this carefulness is that one should not say blessings and prayers hurriedly and truncated, lest he fail to fulfill his obligation, in which case it turns out he mentioned the Name in vain, besides being left without prayer and enjoying benefit without a blessing. And let him clothe himself in dread when mentioning Heaven's Name, all his bones trembling, for all the upper realms shake and tremble when they mention the awesome and fearsome Name. And how good it is, from time to time, to give heart and eyes to look at the order of Keter Malchut and the sanctifications of the Yom Kippur prayers, so as to learn to fear the honored and awesome Name and know a little of the Name's honor from its own place.
Pele Yoetz 352:5: And it is known what our master ruled in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim, sec. 5), that upon mentioning the Name YHVH, one should intend that He was, is, and will be, and upon reading it as Adnut [Adonai], one should intend that He is Master of all, and upon mentioning the Name El Elohim, one should intend that He is mighty, the Master of ability. And it is revealed before Heaven that we are like drunkards because of the distractions of the times and because of the adversary who besets us, which is the evil inclination in the company of turbid matter, and because of the disease of the impurity of our sins' filth, and “you have defiled the land of the peoples” — these withhold good from us to the point that we cannot direct our minds. In any case, an obligation rests upon us to choose the lesser evil and to strengthen ourselves to have intention on the day we can, at the time we can, in the mention we can, and to do all that is in our power to do, and to receive good reward for our toil, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted. And our sages, of blessed memory, explained the verse (Genesis 39:3), “And his master saw that the Lord was with him and that the Lord made all that he did prosper in his hand,” that Heaven's Name was fluent in his mouth (Tanchuma, Vayeshev 7). And Isaac our father recognized “the voice, the voice of Jacob,” because he mentioned Heaven's Name and said (Genesis 27:20), “Because the Lord your God brought it before me.” Behold, therefore, it is good for a man to have Heaven's Name fluent in his mouth with every utterance: if he tells of something he did, let him say, “I did this with the help of Heaven”; and if he tells of something he shall do, let him say, “I shall do this with the help of the blessed Name” — and through this the Name shall make it prosper in his hand.
Pele Yoetz 352:6: We have learned (Avot 2:12): let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven, for through this he gains that all his deeds shall be counted as a commandment and he shall receive good reward for them. And how good it is to utter with his lips, over every single utterance, that he preface by saying that he does it for the needs of the service of the blessed Name, provided that his deeds match what he says with his mouth — that he not go out of line and not increase his business dealings beyond what is necessary for the service of the blessed Name, and not neglect his Creator's service because of his business dealings, and not do anything in his business against his Maker's will (as I have written above under the entry Hachanah), but rather let all his deeds be according to the law of the Torah, in measure, weight, and proportion — let him weigh with a scale everything he does, and he shall receive good reward for every thought, utterance, and deed.
Pele Yoetz 353:1: Shekidah (Diligence) — Great diligence is needed to learn the wisdom of Torah, as it is written (Proverbs 24:10), “If you falter in a day of trouble, your strength is small.” And likewise, to learn any wisdom requires diligence, and likewise to enter into fear of the Name and love of Him and to conduct oneself with good traits and uprightness requires diligence: to study ethical books that teach a person knowledge, or to hear teachings day by day and night by night — in the end their light shall turn him toward the good, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:2), “My teaching shall drip like rain.” Just as constant dripping of rain wears away stone, so those who are diligent with ethical books — they pierce the heart, if it is soft like wax; if it is like iron, it shatters (Kiddushin 30b). But if one studies ethical and God-fearing books or hears teachings only once in a jubilee, he neither ails nor senses it, and it makes no impression on him, and even if it makes an impression for a time, it soon passes and its impression is not recognizable and bears no fruit. And whoever increases his engagement in study and contemplation of ethical books and fear of the Name, and in hearing teachings, so shall his wisdom increase, and his fear of sin, and his cleaving to the Lord, and the perfection of his traits, while according to the smallness of his effort, his acquisition shall be diminished.
Pele Yoetz 353:2: And likewise regarding prayers and supplications, the man who is diligent to pour out speech and speak supplications day by day, in the end his prayer bears fruit, especially if he prays for the desires of Heaven or for the sake of Heaven. And likewise it is written in Sefer Chasidim (sec. 130, 131) that even one who is not worthy of having the Holy One, blessed be He, grant his request — since he increases supplications or asks regarding the desires of Heaven, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall surely hear his outcry. Behold, therefore, happy is the man who heeds being diligent at the gates of contemplation and the study of ethical books, and pours out his speech before the Name — truly, “the righteous in the land shall be repaid” through this.
Pele Yoetz 353:3: And they already said in the Midrash (Yerushalmi Berachot 9:5; Sifrei, Eikev 11:22): the Torah said, “If you forsake me for a day, I shall forsake you for two days.” And would that through such great diligence and effort we could attain a little of the wisdom of Torah, fear of the Name, and perfection of traits, for we have grown exceedingly poor in this orphaned generation, especially regarding the service of thought — to fear and love the honored and awesome Name and cling to Him. And to think thoughts that produce humility and perfection of traits is a service requiring great effort and diligence, and this was the merit of the patriarchs of the world, Moses our teacher, King David, and all the holy ones who are in the land, who were diligent in pure thoughts and great cleaving all day and all night. And they already said (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Rabbah 25) that every person is obligated to say, “When shall my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?” And although we have grown exceedingly poor, let us do what is in our power to do, not to turn to our own understanding nor let our hearts turn to idleness, and the Lord God shall help us.
Pele Yoetz 354:1: Shachen (Neighbor) — King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 27:10), “Better a close neighbor than a distant brother.” And a good neighbor is beneficial for a time of joy and a time of sorrow, and at a time of trouble, help in troubles is very much found. And it is fitting for a person to seek to dwell among good neighbors. And it is known, the statement of the Tanna (Avot 1:7): distance yourself from a bad neighbor. And likewise they instituted for us to pray every day before the Name that He save us from a bad neighbor, for many are the deeds of bad neighbors. And they said (Sukkah 56b): woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbor; good to the righteous, good to his neighbor. For when the neighbor is bad, even if one is not drawn after him and does not learn from his ways and does not speak forbidden words with him, it cannot be avoided that his eyes shall see and his ears shall hear his bad speech and corrupt ways, and he cannot protest at every time and every hour, and in the end he shall be burned by his coals, and his encounter shall be bad, for it increases dispute every day and every hour over trivial matters. Behold, therefore, the man who desires life should not be concerned with its inner details, and it is good to dwell in the corner of a roof rather than sit with a good neighbor — no, rather, it is good to sit with a good neighbor: each shall help his fellow in worldly matters and heavenly matters, and it is good for him with him.
Pele Yoetz 354:2: And among the conditions for neighbors who wish to dwell in love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, is that they not burden each other by one entering his fellow's house at all times and prolonging his stay there, unless they know for certain that both are content with brothers dwelling together. And one should not burden his fellow by asking many questions, only at a time of great need when it is impossible for him to acquire it in any other way, and he cannot do without it. And when he asks, let the other hasten to return it or pay in full, better an hour sooner, in the manner and way in which he lent it, not lesser or dirtier, and let neither be resentful of the other over trivial matters, and how much more so should he bear his fellow's burden and help him with his body and his money at his time of joy and his time of trouble. And when the man is not in his house, his neighbor near his house shall watch over his house, and from time to time they shall mingle and sit like brothers dwelling together to stir the blood of love. And if something is missing from his house, he should not ask his neighbor whether he saw or knew of it, in a manner that would make his neighbor think he suspects him, but rather show him and clarify his own suspicions to inform him that he has no suspicion of him. And it is best that each guard himself from his neighbor, for they have already said regarding every person: suspect him like a robber but honor him like the head of the exile. And people say: close your door and praise your neighbor.
Pele Yoetz 354:3: And included in the good of neighborliness is that they not be too closely attached in one courtyard or one house, for with great difficulty could they escape dispute, especially among women, who are quarrelsome, so that dispute is almost unavoidable, as I have written above under the entry Machloket. Therefore it is best that each be in his own courtyard, with an open doorway from his courtyard to his fellow's with a lock, so that when they wish they open it and when they wish they close it. And just as one must investigate a neighbor to ensure he is a good man, even more so must one investigate a neighbor's wife to ensure she is a good woman with good traits, one who desires kindness and loves peace, for she is the mistress of the house, and upon these depends the love of neighbors, as it is known that every man is bound to his wife. And the wisdom of women: a God-fearing woman, even if she has some resentment or dispute with her neighbor or her mother-in-law or her sister-in-law, should not tell her husband, for if this causes dispute, her deeds are wrongful, since dispute is hated, as I have written above, and that woman shall bear her own sin, for fire shall go out and burn her with her own coals; but if she seeks peace and increases peace, peace shall be hers and no plague shall come near her tent.
Pele Yoetz 355:1: Shir (Song) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesikta Rabbati 26) regarding the verse (Proverbs 3:9), “Honor the Lord with your wealth” — with your grace, meaning if one has a pleasant voice, let him give his grace before his Maker for his Maker's honor, and for this one must gather great strength and courage not to intend that it be pleasant to the listeners, but let his deeds be for the sake of Heaven, specifically for the honor of the blessed Name. And they already told of a pious man who heard the voice of a cantor singing in the synagogue with great pleasantness, and they asked him whether it was pleasant to him, and he answered, “It is neither pleasant to me nor right in my eyes, because I see that he does it so that it be pleasant to me, and not for the sake of Heaven.” And this is an exceedingly difficult thing, almost impossible to withstand, except through great strength and by persisting in thinking, “What does it give me and what does it add to me whether it is pleasant to the listeners or not?” And it is already written in the books that whatever begins for the sake of Heaven, even if afterward his heart swells with pride over people delighting in his voice, there is no objection. And how good it is if he sets his heart on the words of the song, for it cannot be avoided that they contain mention of the Name's kindnesses and supplications for the building of the Holy Temple and atonement for sins — over this let him pray in his singing from the depths of his heart's walls and not turn to arrogance.
Pele Yoetz 355:2: And the halachic authorities already wrote that one whose voice is not pleasant to listeners should not sing loudly, for it shall not be accepted with favor before the Name, since “your grace” is required. And let him choose to sing the songs of King David, peace be upon him, with clear speech and pleasantness, and it shall be very acceptable before the Name, for He is the one who chose David His servant and his songs above all the songs in the world, for they are the words of the living God spoken to King David through the holy spirit. However, if the Name has graced him with a pleasant voice, let him hold to this and also to that, and let him sing at the head of the watches and in the synagogue before the morning prayer, for it is written (I Kings 8:28), “To hear the song and the prayer.” Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 6a): in the place of song, there shall be prayer. Learn from this that one must say songs and praises in the synagogue, and especially on Shabbatot and festivals it is fitting to increase songs in the synagogue.
Pele Yoetz 355:3: And let everyone sing at his table pleasant songs relevant to the matter of the day — a matter in its proper time, how good it is — and this is an exceedingly important service of the Name that all the angels on high and the entire host on high employ, and this is their service, and all of them open their mouths in song and melody, as we say in Yotzer, and all the creatures of the world say song, as is written in Perek Shirah. And the sages of the generations, in every generation, have already composed songs, praises, and requests in the holy tongue, and for those who speak a foreign vernacular, in that vernacular, by the thousands and myriads — whoever wishes to take may take, and choose to sing from them according to his means, day by day, and it is a merit for him that he grants merit to those who composed them, that their wellsprings be dispersed abroad, and that their lips move in the grave, and their merit shall protect us.
Pele Yoetz 355:4: And it is already written in Sefer Chasidim (section 114) that whoever discontinues the Kerovetz [liturgical poems] customarily recited in the synagogue transgresses “do not remove the ancient boundary” (Proverbs 22:28), and he is in danger of dying, Heaven forbid. Therefore let every man guard his soul, and even those piyyutim [liturgical poems] that some places are accustomed to recite on the Days of Awe in the middle of Yotzer, and it is fitting to discontinue the custom, one should not uproot them entirely but rather move them to be said after the repetition of the Amidah. And it is good for a man to strive to compose songs, praises, and requests himself, according to his means, for then they shall be dear to him, since a person favors his own measure, and let him not fail to recite them; and if he merits that his songs spread among the many, happy is he and happy is his portion, for his righteousness shall stand forever and his lips shall move in the grave — and this is a gift of God, according to a person's deeds and his cleaving to his Maker (and the Name has already granted me His goodness and I have merited to compose some requests and songs, a matter in its proper time, and I have included them in my House of Prayers, with the help of Heaven — may the Name desire me and grant me that my wellsprings be dispersed abroad, and that I too be built up through the kindness of God).
Pele Yoetz 355:5: And just as it is good to give thanks to the Lord and sing songs and praises, correspondingly there is a great prohibition against singing foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation, especially over wine, for he transgresses what is written (Isaiah 24:9), “With song they shall not drink wine.” And through our sins, this scab has spread in some places, especially among young men in joyful company, and among men this is their foolish way, to sing foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation — woe to the eyes that see such things and the ears that hear such things. And our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Sotah 48a): an ear that hears song shall be uprooted. They further said (ibid.): song in the house, the sword outside. And the masses of the people do not know that there is a prohibition and its severity. And it is fitting for the leaders of cities to stand in the breach and inform them and separate them from this prohibition, for they said in the Talmud (ibid.) that when Rav Huna abolished song, a hundred geese cost a zuz and a hundred se'ah of wheat cost a zuz and were not wanted; when Rav Chisda came and treated it lightly [reinstated it], a goose could not be found for a zuz.
Pele Yoetz 355:6: Behold, therefore, it is fitting for the leaders of cities to have regard for their cities so that the blessing of the Name be found among them. But what shall the leaders of the generation do, since their generation is not favorable, for even if a thousand sages expound a thousand thousand expositions that foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation are forbidden, the women and young men do not heed them, either because they do not believe and laugh at them, or because they cannot subdue their inclination to abandon their bad custom, since they do not know songs and praises of the Name — in these their tongues were trained, and what shall they sing at celebrations and joyous occasions? And would that they were wise and understood that their silence would be better. And let them call singers, male or female, who know how to sing songs of Torah, which are thanksgivings to the Lord and requests, and absence is better than the presence of evil. And they think to perform a commandment, such as gladdening a groom and bride and the like, yet a transgression is in their hand, for they defile their mouths and blemish it, and would that joy not turn to sorrow, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid.): song in the house, etc. And seeing that the sages of the generation are not heeded, the modest ones withdraw their hands from rebuking over every matter of transgression, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 148b): leave Israel be, better that they be unwitting sinners than deliberate ones. But the man who knows that his wife and household members are God-fearing and heed his words should warn them with seven warnings not to hear foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation from anyone anywhere, and all the more so should he not allow them to be sung in his house under any circumstances, and through this no evil shall befall him and no plague shall come near his tent, and peace shall be within his ranks.
Pele Yoetz 355:7: And whoever the Name has graced with a pleasant voice, if he uses it to sing for a matter of transgression, this is comparable to one whom the king honored with fine clothing so that he adorn himself with it when coming before him, and he instead dresses his dog in it — the king shall be exceedingly angry. And if these bad songs are written in his own ledger, so shall they be written in the ledger on high and read before Him at the time of judgment, and for all this shall God bring into judgment.
Pele Yoetz 355:8: And this is a grievous evil, that among these matters that many have trampled upon and treated as entirely permitted — such as these bad songs, and the prohibition of idle words, and the prohibition of neglecting Torah even for a moment when free, and the like — when the wise man expounds to them and says, “This is a great sin and a criminal offense,” they say, “How this sage burdens us, wishing to make us ascetics from this world like ministering angels — who can withstand fulfilling his words? We have found the world thus from ancient days and former years, and thus it is accustomed, and thus is the custom of the whole world; whatever happens to them shall happen to us.” But would that a soul would come from that world, as one came to Rabbeinu Yechiel and told him how they are exacting and how they judge in that world regarding any matter of transgression, even the width of a hair, and how much more so forbidden things like these — for whoever believes the words of our sages, of blessed memory, the holy ones, that they are true and their words are true, shall certainly admit that these are criminal offenses whose punishment is severe, bad and bitter. And upon whom shall we rely? Upon our Father in Heaven — He, in His mercies, shall plant in the heart of His people Israel love and fear of Him, to do His will as His will and to heed the words of the wise, for their own good, Amen, so may it be [His] will.
Pele Yoetz 356:1: Shaliach Tzibbur (Prayer Leader) — Our master, in the Shulchan Aruch, section 53, already clarified the laws of the prayer leader. And in the book Shalmei Tzibbur he elaborated at length on the conditions required of a prayer leader. And truly it is difficult to find a prayer leader perfect in every respect as required, but in any case it is fitting for the leaders of communities not to appoint a prayer leader except through a wise man who at least knows how to choose the lesser evil. And at the very least the prayer leader should be learned, and through this understand what comes from his mouth, and also know how to study the books that speak of the obligations of the prayer leader, and go over them at least once a month so as not to be blemished and cause blemish, for he is like a priest standing to atone for the people, and if the anointed priest sins, it is to the guilt of the people.
Pele Yoetz 356:2: And he must be more careful than the entire congregation of Israel not to blemish his mouth with any forbidden speech, lest he draw near to serve with an impure and dirty vessel. And he should also contemplate repentance before his prayer, so that it not be said of him, “The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination,” Heaven forbid. And let him strive with all his might to have intention in his prayer and not to stumble in his speech, for they said (Berachot 34b) that a prayer leader who errs is a bad sign for those who sent him. Therefore let him not rush through his prayer, and especially in the Torah reading he must be very careful to read it as it was given at Sinai, with its grammatical precision and its cantillation. And he should not heed the voice of those who whisper and rush him to hurry — he should not heed them nor agree with them, for it is a sin borne by the many, and he should not bring his bread [i.e., earn favor] at the cost of his own soul, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent. And these matters have a proper measure — he should not be overly prolonged and deliberate, nor overly hasty, but a proper medium. And let him give his grace before his Maker to sing on Shabbatot and festivals and at joyous occasions as the Name has graced him, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven, for the Rabbi Kenesset HaGedolah wrote that a prayer leader who intends to let his voice be heard and delights in his own voice, regarding him it is said (Jeremiah 12:8), “She has given forth her voice against me, therefore I have hated her.” And let him honor everyone equally, rich and poor alike.
Pele Yoetz 356:3: And the prayer leader, and anyone who serves the public, must not be irritable and must overlook his own grievances more than anyone else, and must be truly humble so that his prayer be heard, and must be sociable with people, doing their will as their will as much as he can, provided there is no nullification of the Creator's will, and in a manner that finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man. And let him not turn to his own benefit, but rather trust in the Name, and make his prayer mercy and supplication before the Divine Presence, and perform his work, the work of Heaven, with faithfulness, and the Name shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 356:4: And above all, let him precede trouble with prayer; every day let him pour out his soul before the Name, that He help him serve in holiness with proper service, and to perform his service as a complete service, a whole service, as is fitting to do. These are some of the aspects of the straight path required of a prayer leader; let the wise man hear and add learning, and study the books that speak of this, and let them not depart from his mouth. Behold, therefore, when appointing a prayer leader, one should not follow those who excel in pleasantness of voice but lack knowledge, for the beauty and vanity of voice are false compared to the other qualities required of a prayer leader. And the prayer leader who has wisdom, whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, and who is perfect in good traits — he shall be praised.
Pele Yoetz 356:5: And especially on the Days of Awe, not everyone who wishes to take the name of prayer leader may take it, for it is the sin of the congregation if the prayer leader is unworthy, since through him comes forgiveness of sin, and he stands as an intermediary between the Name and the people, and “when the shepherd is angry at the flock, he appoints a blind guide for them” (Bava Kamma 52a), and then the whole flock goes astray, they stumble and fall, Heaven forbid. Behold, therefore, it is fitting to choose the wisest and most God-fearing man in the congregation to be the prayer leader for the prayers of the mighty days. And let me tell the generation an awesome incident I heard, that once on Yom Kippur a certain pious kabbalist prayed and created a wondrous arousal, such that all the people contemplated complete repentance, and afterward the mentioned pious man revealed that they had already been aroused in the heavenly court to send Israel's redemption, and the attribute of judgment prosecuted and said: “It is true that all the people contemplated repentance, but the anointed priest [the prayer leader] sinned in that he did not pray with great humility as is fitting to do,” and because of this the exile returned to its full force through our many sins. Hear this, prayer leaders and those who appoint them, and take to heart who is fit to be a prayer leader, and how one must conduct oneself so that the Holy One, blessed be He, hear all the prayers of His people Israel with mercy and inscribe them in the Book of Good Life.
Pele Yoetz 357:1: Shemirah (Guarding) — It is written (Deuteronomy 4:15), “And you shall greatly guard your souls,” and it is written (ibid.), “Only take heed to yourself and guard your soul greatly.” Look and see that no other commandment is stated with “greatly” as with this commandment, that a person is obligated to guard his soul from danger and from possible danger. And the reason is that one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17). And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 32a): a person should never enter a place of danger, saying, “They shall perform a miracle for me,” for perhaps they shall not perform a miracle for him, and if they do perform a miracle for him, they deduct from his merits. And in the holy Zohar they said regarding the verse (Proverbs 22:3), “The shrewd man sees evil and hides himself, but the simple pass on and are punished” — meaning that for this alone, that they did not hide themselves, even if they have no other sin, they are punished, since he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Deuteronomy 4:15), “And you shall greatly guard your souls.” And I saw among the commentators, regarding that pious man in the Talmud (Berachot 32b) who was standing in prayer and a governor encountered him and greeted him, and he did not return the greeting, etc., and said to him, “Wait for me until I appease you with words,” and he appeased him with words, and it says there that pious man departed to his house — the commentators explained that he departed to his eternal home, since in any case he transgressed what is written in the Torah, “And you shall guard,” for perhaps the governor would not have spoken with him and would have cut off his head. It turns out that whoever places himself in a place of danger and relies on a miracle has done himself two evils: one, that he shall be punished for transgressing “And you shall guard”; and further, that they deduct from his merits — and this is like exchanging a pearl and a precious stone for the value of a penny. Behold, therefore, it is fitting for a person to guard his soul greatly from every suspicion of danger, and not walk the roads and not enter seas and rivers unless out of great necessity, not for the sake of the slightest monetary gain. And whoever forgoes money to guard his soul and not enter a place of danger, it shall be counted as a great commandment expense.
Pele Yoetz 357:2: And when there is plague in the city, Heaven forbid, let him fulfill the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Bava Kamma 60b), “Gather in your feet,” or let him flee and his soul shall be as spoil to him, as it is written (Isaiah 26:20), “Hide for a brief moment until the indignation passes.” And let a person not say, in the manner of the foolish Ishmaelites who say (Psalms 127:1), “If the Lord does not guard the city, the watchman guards in vain” — and nothing is hidden from His wrath, and none can save from His hand — it is written (Jeremiah 16:19), “Surely our fathers have inherited falsehood,” for He commanded “and you shall guard,” and it is written (Isaiah 26:20), “Go, my people, enter your chambers.” And the resolution to this I have written above under the entry Refuah — see there — that there are three kinds of decrees, and we do not know, and it falls upon us to do what is incumbent upon us, and the Name shall do what is good in His eyes.
Pele Yoetz 357:3: And included in the obligation of guarding is, how much more so, the obligation to guard against every transgression and every evil thing, for they said (Berachot 11a) to Rabbi Tarfon: you would have deserved to be liable for your own life, for you transgressed the words of Beit Hillel. And we have learned (Avot 3:4): one who stays awake at night, or walks alone on the road, and turns his heart to idleness, is liable for his own soul. And we have also learned (ibid., mishnah 8): whoever forgets a single word of his study, Scripture accounts it to him as though he were liable for his own soul. And the same applies to every matter of transgression and sin a person commits and thereby becomes liable for death at the hand of Heaven — if he dies, his own blood and the blood of his offspring he could have fathered shall his Creator demand from his hand, and for all this shall God bring into judgment: for the commandments he could have fulfilled and the children he could have fathered. Let the man tremble and shrink at this too, and be careful to withdraw his hand from every evil thing and guard every good thing, so as not to cause death to himself or his offspring, Heaven forbid. And they said in the Talmud (Shabbat 129a) that whoever is lenient with himself regarding the meal after bloodletting, not eating and drinking much, his food allowance is reduced [in Heaven], and they say, “He has no regard for his own life; shall we have regard for him?” From this we learn regarding anyone who, for any monetary gain, places himself in a place of danger, or who is exceedingly frugal with his expenses and is distressed and suffers and does not guard his health — he thinks to profit but loses more, for they reduce his food allowance and say, “He has no regard for his own life,” etc. And in the way a person wishes to go, they lead him — to one who spends, they give from Heaven so that he can spend, while to one who is stingy and frugal and content with little, they give him little — unless he is stingy and reduces his expenses in order to increase commandments and good deeds all the more, in which case his portion is good; he eats the fruits in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 357:4: And included in guarding is that one should not guard himself excessively, nor neglect his Creator's service by saying, “There is a lion on the road, in the streets,” and likewise he should not neglect his Creator's service to protect himself from the heat because of the heat, or from the cold because of the cold. And if he wishes to eat to satiety, distending his belly, and drink much wine, and sleep the sleep of the morning and the sleep of the afternoon, time after time, even though he says he does this for the sake of Heaven, to guard his soul and health, this is nothing but the counsel of the evil inclination. This is like the parable of the fox who told the fish to come out onto dry land to flee and escape the fishermen, and the fish gave him a decisive answer: if we are afraid in the place of our life, how much more so in the place of our death. And it is written (Ecclesiastes 8:5), “Whoever guards a commandment shall know no evil thing.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 39b): agents on a mission of a commandment are not harmed, neither on their going nor on their returning. And if some harm should befall a person while performing a commandment, let him believe what they said in the Talmud (Shabbat 118b): Rav Yosef said, “May my portion be among those who die on the way of performing a commandment,” for his death is his atonement and he is destined for the life of the World to Come. But where harm is common, it is different — such as a rickety ladder, or a place of gangs of wild beasts and robbers — then let him withdraw his hand and forgo the commandment, for the Merciful One said, “And he shall live by them” (Leviticus 18:5). And a scale and balances of justice are needed to conduct his affairs with judgment: he should not overguard where they said to be lenient, nor be lenient where they said to be strict about guarding. This is the rule: any harm likely to come through natural means, or through a person acting of his own free will, one should not rely on a miracle even in performing a commandment, and should not do anything outside of nature; but regarding other concerns, he should not worry at all, but rather trust in the Name and lean on his God that no evil shall befall him while he guards a commandment for the sake of Heaven. And if it happens that he is compelled by circumstances to enter a place of danger and cannot escape, let him precede trouble with prayer before the Name, that He perform a miracle for him according to His mercies and kindnesses from the treasury of free gifts, and let Him not deduct from his merits, and then his heart shall be steadfast, trusting in the Lord, his heart upheld, he shall not fear nor be afraid, as I have written above under the entry Pachad — see there.
Pele Yoetz 357:5: And one must be careful regarding everything found written in books that involves danger, and “whoever despises a matter shall be injured by it”, and happy is the man who fears always, and whoever hardens his heart shall fall into evil, Heaven forbid. And it is good for a man to walk in innocence, walking securely, and not search to know what are the bad and harmful things for the body, for perhaps he cannot guard against them and his heart shall fear and he shall fall into evil, Heaven forbid; but since he does not know, no evil shall befall him, for “the Lord guards the simple” (Psalms 116:6), and “he who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him,” and He shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 358:1: Sechok (Laughter/Levity) — We have learned (Avot 3:11): laughter and levity accustom a person to lewdness. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 31a): it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world. And through our sins, there are people who delight in laughter, and there are wealthy people who cultivate the jesters of the generation among them, who know how to speak humor and open their mouths in much laughter and great merriment, and the speaker's heart swells with pride that he has merited having the wealthy laugh at his words, and he digs and searches within himself for more to say and to do words of frivolity, laughter, and levity, so that they laugh and rejoice more. And this matter is especially common among women and fools, and all their words are like burning coals of broom, for they increase speaking obscene words and mocking their fellow creatures — woe to those who speak and alas to those who laugh; together they shall all pass through the Valley of Weeping, making it a place of springs, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Eruvin 19a) that they weep in Gehinnom and shed rivers and streams of tears — this shall be the fruit of their joy over a matter of transgression. And our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Avodah Zarah 18b) that mockery begins with suffering and ends in destruction, may the Merciful One save us.
Pele Yoetz 358:2: Behold, therefore, let one who guards his soul distance himself from such people and not act as they do. And if a poor man should say that he does these things so that people will open their hand to him, since there are wealthy people who open their hands more to give to such men than to what they give to poor people of good family, and so that they can sit at the head of the invited guests in the houses of the wealthy — this too is vanity, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.
Pele Yoetz 358:3: And there is another kind of laughter, bad and bitter, namely those who play at dice and vain games and card games and the like — all kinds of gambling are bad and sinful, and they cause much evil: first, that this is a session of scoffers, and these people have forsaken the Name, spurned the Holy One of Israel, in that they waste many hours of precious time to anger their Creator, in a place where they could have acquired, during that time, life in the World to Come had they engaged in Torah. And furthermore, there is a concern of robbery, since a mere undertaking [asmachta] does not effect acquisition, and our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 24b) that they are disqualified from testimony. Therefore the God-fearing person should bind himself with a firm resolution and not play any game at all, but rather let his desire always be in the Torah of the Name.
Pele Yoetz 358:4: And regarding this too, many are unrestrained, for whom this is their foolish way and their occupation, wasting many nights and many days in gambling in houses, gardens, and street corners, sinking much money and many souls into it, to the point that some destroy their wealth even if their means were great, for everything has an end, and in the end they rob and extort while the members of their household lie in hunger, their children asking for bread with none to give them, since they do not occupy themselves with settling the world to bring sustenance to their house. And one transgression drags along another, for they neglect prayers and commandments, since at the time the evil inclination overpowers them and they stand at their gambling, it is as hard for them to part from it as separating a fingernail from the flesh, and they have no regard for their own lives, and do not free themselves from gambling even to eat at mealtime or sleep at bedtime. And whoever is habituated to the bad custom of gambling, even when he grows old shall not depart from it, unless a man gathers strength, and with the help of the Almighty opens his eyes and awakens from his sleep of folly, and says, “Woe is me, how I destroy my body, my soul, and my money, and consume precious time in vanity and confusion, and cause my body and soul many troubles and evils in this world and the World to Come — am I lacking compared to madmen, that I have no regard for my own soul and my own honor” (for whoever does these things is despised and loathsome, abominable and filthy in people's eyes) “and for my Maker's honor, and why should I not be master of my own spirit? Is it not that whatever a man desires, he can do,” and it is in his power to rectify this before the sun grows dark and before the days of evil come. Such and such things let the living take to heart regarding every matter of transgression, to rectify his distortion, and especially regarding bad things he is habituated to, such as gambling and drunkenness and other bad traits and bad deeds he has trampled upon and treated as permitted — let him gather strength like a mighty man of valor and like a man of war to save his soul from descending to the pit.
Pele Yoetz 358:5: And immediately upon his arousal, let him go to a sage to rectify him with good counsel, whether it is fitting and proper for him to take a vow upon his own soul and fence himself in with strength through bribery-like inducements [self-imposed incentives], in the manner of what is written (Psalms 119:106), “I have sworn and confirmed, to keep Your righteous ordinances.” For not everyone who wishes to swear can swear, but rather according to what the wise man sees fit: whether it is necessary, or whether there are other, better fences; and whether it is fitting to rely on the fact that, once he swears, he can withstand it and not transgress his oath; and whether it is fitting for him to leave a measure and time for leniency, or that he be forbidden that thing entirely, completely, forever. In all this let him not depart from whatever the wise man tells him, right or left; if he does so, then he shall succeed in his affairs and then he shall have understanding.
Pele Yoetz 359:1: Shemi'ah (Hearing) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Isaiah 55:3), “Hear, and your soul shall live.” Come and see that the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the attribute of flesh and blood. The attribute of flesh and blood: a person who fell from a roof and his entire body was filled with wounds — the doctor comes to him and fills his entire body with bandages. But the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so; rather, a person full of sins — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, “Place a bandage on the ear, and the whole body is healed.” This is what is written, “Hear, and your soul shall live.” And our sages, of blessed memory, further said (Midrash Mishlei ch. 10; Kohelet Rabbah ch. 9) that whoever listens with affection to the words of the wise man who sits and expounds, and answers “Yehei shmei rabba” which is said over words of Aggadah, they tear up for him a decree of seventy years and forgive him all his sins (Shabbat 119b).
Pele Yoetz 359:2: And the reason hearing is so important is in the manner they said (Kiddushin 40b): great is study that leads to action. So hearing leads to action more than studying, for hearing has more effect than one who has a fluent tongue and expounds with broad, eloquent speech, more than if he studied ethical books himself. And a sign for this matter: “Hear, my son, instruction.” And since the evil inclination sees the great merit of hearing words of ethics and words of Aggadah — that whatever it gains, it loses through a person hearing words of ethics, since through hearing his sins are forgiven and he returns to the good — it therefore entices him with double persuasion to hate rebukes and be disgusted by them and not go to the wise, and through this “the way of a fool is upright in his own eyes,” for the evil inclination has flattered him with the smoothness of its tongue to make him think he is perfect in everything, a mighty man among the mighty, cleansed of sin, since the severe transgressions he has trampled upon have become treated as permitted for him, and his heart does not ache and he does not take it to heart to repent.
